metadata.title: The effects of individual- and class-level achievement on attitudes towards mathematics: An analysis of Hong Kong students using TIMSS 2019

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 microdata for Hong Kong, restricting the analytic sample to fourth- and eighth-graders in mathematics classrooms and then aggregating class-level achievement as the classroom reference (average class achievement). The authors report deleting observations with missing data using listwise deletion when creating the multilevel data matrix for HLM, but they do not report applying TIMSS sampling weights or replicate weights in the analysis. Because the analysis is conducted with two-level hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) rather than ML algorithms, the manuscript does not provide a weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or any complex-survey design adjustment details. As a result, the weighting strategy for population-representative inference is unclear from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 Hong Kong mathematics classrooms and restricted the sample to fourth- and eighth-graders. The analytic sample was created after deleting observations with missing data (listwise deletion) when constructing the multilevel data matrix for HLM. The study further operationalized class-level achievement using average class mathematics achievement (classroom mean) as the classroom-level reference, and it analyzed outcomes separately for fourth grade and eighth grade.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized coefficients): Individual math achievement β = 0.44 (p < .001); Gender β = 0.34 (p < .001); SES β = 0.01 (ns); Class average math achievement β = −0.23 (p < .001). Cross-level moderation: Individual math achievement × class average math achievement β = 0.06 (p < .01); Gender × class average math achievement β = 0.06 (ns).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics data for Hong Kong, the study leveraged individual math achievement, gender, SES, and class average math achievement to predict students’ self-concept (ATM), finding that higher individual achievement was associated with higher self-concept (β = 0.44, p < .001) while higher class average achievement was associated with lower self-concept (β = −0.23, p < .001). This indicates that the big-fish-little-pond effect extends beyond achievement to students’ competence beliefs, suggesting that classroom composition and peer-achievement context should be considered when designing supports for students’ self-concept.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized coefficients): Individual math achievement β = 0.35 (p < .001); Gender β = 0.28 (p < .001); SES β = −0.01 (ns); Class average math achievement β = −0.17 (p < .001). Cross-level moderation: Individual math achievement × class average math achievement β = 0.03 (ns); Gender × class average math achievement β = 0.05 (ns).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics data for Hong Kong, the study leveraged individual math achievement, gender, SES, and class average math achievement to predict enjoyment (ATM), finding that higher individual achievement was associated with greater enjoyment (β = 0.35, p < .001) while higher class average achievement was associated with lower enjoyment (β = −0.17, p < .001). This indicates that peer-achievement context can dampen positive affect even when students themselves perform well, suggesting that teachers should monitor enjoyment in high-achieving classrooms and provide engagement supports rather than assuming high achievement automatically yields positive attitudes.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized coefficients): Individual math achievement β = −0.33 (p < .001); Gender β = −0.13 (p < .001); SES β = 0.01 (ns); Class average math achievement β = 0.15 (p < .001). Cross-level moderation: Individual math achievement × class average math achievement β = 0.01 (ns); Gender × class average math achievement β = −0.07 (ns).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics data for Hong Kong, the study leveraged individual math achievement, gender, SES, and class average math achievement to predict boredom (ATM), finding that higher individual achievement was associated with less boredom (β = −0.33, p < .001) while higher class average achievement was associated with more boredom (β = 0.15, p < .001). This indicates that high-achieving classroom environments may increase negative affect through social comparison processes, suggesting that classroom-level interventions (e.g., differentiated pacing and cognitive activation) may be needed to reduce boredom in top-track settings.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized coefficients): Individual math achievement β = 0.58 (p < .001); Gender β = 0.34 (p < .001); SES β = −0.01 (ns); Class average math achievement β = −0.42 (p < .001). Cross-level moderation: Individual math achievement × class average math achievement β = 0.10 (p < .001); Gender × class average math achievement β = 0.06 (ns).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics data for Hong Kong, the study leveraged individual math achievement, gender, SES, and class average math achievement to predict self-concept (ATM), finding that higher individual achievement was associated with higher self-concept (β = 0.58, p < .001) while higher class average achievement was associated with lower self-concept (β = −0.42, p < .001). This indicates that the big-fish-little-pond effect becomes stronger in later grades, suggesting that schools should anticipate larger peer-context risks to students’ competence beliefs as students move into more demanding mathematics instruction.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized coefficients): Individual math achievement β = 0.38 (p < .001); Gender β = 0.15 (p < .001); SES β = 0.02 (ns); Class average math achievement β = −0.16 (p < .001). Cross-level moderation: Individual math achievement × class average math achievement β = 0.01 (ns); Gender × class average math achievement β = −0.01 (ns).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics data for Hong Kong, the study leveraged individual math achievement, gender, SES, and class average math achievement to predict perceived value (ATM), finding that higher individual achievement was associated with higher perceived value (β = 0.38, p < .001) while higher class average achievement was associated with lower perceived value (β = −0.16, p < .001). This indicates that peer-achievement context can erode students’ perceived usefulness of mathematics, suggesting that value-building strategies (e.g., connecting math to real-life goals) may be especially important in high-achieving classrooms.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized coefficients): Individual math achievement β = 0.57 (p < .001); Gender β = 0.25 (p < .001); SES β = −0.01 (ns); Class average math achievement β = −0.37 (p < .001). Cross-level moderation: Individual math achievement × class average math achievement β = 0.03 (ns); Gender × class average math achievement β = 0.05 (ns).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics data for Hong Kong, the study leveraged individual math achievement, gender, SES, and class average math achievement to predict enjoyment (ATM), finding that higher individual achievement was associated with greater enjoyment (β = 0.57, p < .001) while higher class average achievement was associated with lower enjoyment (β = −0.37, p < .001). This indicates that the negative peer-context effect on positive affect is substantial in eighth grade, suggesting that teachers should actively sustain enjoyment in high-achieving classrooms through supportive instruction and opportunities for meaningful understanding.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level HLM (standardized coefficients): Individual math achievement β = −0.47 (p < .001); Gender β = −0.13 (p < .001); SES β = −0.01 (ns); Class average math achievement β = 0.32 (p < .001). Cross-level moderation: Gender × class average math achievement β = −0.08 (p < .05); Individual math achievement × class average math achievement β = −0.05 (p < .001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics data for Hong Kong, the study leveraged individual math achievement, gender, SES, and class average math achievement to predict boredom (ATM), finding that higher individual achievement was associated with less boredom (β = −0.47, p < .001) while higher class average achievement was associated with more boredom (β = 0.32, p < .001), with moderation indicating stronger boredom-related peer-context effects for girls and for lower-performing students. This indicates that classroom-level achievement context interacts with student gender and ability to shape negative affect, suggesting that differentiated emotional and instructional support should target girls and lower-achieving students in high-performing math classrooms.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzed TIMSS 2019 Hong Kong mathematics data for fourth- and eighth-graders (N = 2,947 and 3,265, respectively) to examine how individual and class-level achievement relate to attitudes toward mathematics (enjoyment, boredom, perceived value, and self-concept). Mathematics achievement was based on five TIMSS plausible values, operationalized as the mean across the five PVs, while attitudes were measured with TIMSS SLM/SCM/SVM items on 4-point Likert scales. Using two-level hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) with listwise deletion for missing data, the authors found a consistent pattern: individual achievement positively predicted all ATM constructs, whereas class average achievement negatively predicted self-concept, value, and enjoyment and positively predicted boredom. The big-fish-little-pond effect was stronger in eighth grade than fourth grade, and moderation showed that gender and individual performance further shaped the class-level achievement–boredom relationship. Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weight usage and the use of cross-sectional associations (no causal identification).
